today.h: The Inverse-Bond Trade: Nasdaq Sets a Record as the 10Y Prints a Fresh 2002 High
today.c1: A record that refused to read the bond market: the Nasdaq closed at an all-time high of 27,477.31 (+1.05%, intraday 27,544.07), the S&P 500 added 0.66% to 7,773.95 — within ~0.3% of its August record — and the Dow lagged at +0.18%. The tape did it while the 10-year yield spiked ~7bp to 5.349%, its highest since April 2002, before closing at 5.311% (+3bp); the 30-year printed 5.703% intraday, a level last seen in May 2002. 'Tech is sort of like the inverse bond trade,' said Infrastructure Capital's Jay Hatfield — 'it's buy tech, sell everything else.' Monday's data was tame (ISM services 54.9, roughly in line; the prices-paid index 74, its 12-month average the highest since March 2023), and the tape took its cues elsewhere: oil's second straight supply-driven slide (Brent -1.9% to $100.32; WTI settled $89.43) softened the inflation edge, the dollar firmed (DXY +0.2%; the euro hit a 17-month low on France's fiscal crisis), and gold settled -0.1% at $4,156.8. Under the record: M&A Monday (Schneider's $22.6B all-cash takeout of PTC — +33.5%, the S&P's top gainer and its biggest one-day gain on record; C.H. Robinson's $5.8B deal for RXO), Brazil's election rip (PBR +11.5%, the real +4%), SpaceX +7.6% — and thin breadth: only ~50.6% of Nasdaq issues advanced.
today.c4:
• Rates still set the terms: the 10Y's 5.31%-5.35% zone is every multiple's ceiling — the record stood Monday, but a break above ~5.35% without earnings proof is the risk; the Fed minutes (Wednesday) and CPI (Oct 14) referee next.
  • Watch breadth, not the index: 50.6% of Nasdaq names advancing under a record close says megacaps are carrying it — the narrowness is the fragility.
  • Oil's supply wave (G7 barrels, recovering exports, Aramco's price cut) is the cleanest disinflation input left; Houthi strikes on Aramco sites are the counter-bid — $100 Brent is the line.

chains.t: ① Main Chain: The Inverse-Bond Trade — a Nasdaq Record While the 10Y Prints a 2002 High
steps: 10:00 ET: ISM services 54.9 for September — roughly in line, slightly below August; prices-paid +1.4 to 74, its 12-month average the highest since March 2023
The long end keeps selling: the 10Y spikes ~7bp to 5.349% — highest since April 3, 2002 — and closes +3bp at 5.311%; the 30Y peaks at 5.703%, best since May 2002
Hatfield: 'It's a momentum selloff' — the 10Y trades ~100bp over terminal Fed funds as fiscal and inflation worries pile up
Equities don't blink: Nasdaq +1.05% to a record close 27,477.31 (intraday 27,544.07); S&P +0.66% to 7,773.95; Dow +0.18%
Megacaps carry: Nvidia +2.1%, Meta +1.9%, Tesla +2.2%, Microsoft +1.5%, SpaceX +7.6% — 'buy tech, sell everything else'
Cross-asset: DXY +0.2% to 102.11 (the euro hit a 17-month low on France); oil -1.9% cushions; gold settles -0.1% at $4,156.8
chains.d: One trade explained Monday's 60%: tech as the inverse bond trade — a record Nasdaq close while the 10-year printed its highest level since 2002, cushioned by an oil slide and a firm dollar.

news.fact: ISM services PMI came in at 54.9 for September — roughly in line with expectations and slightly below August; the prices-paid index rose 1.4 points to 74, putting its 12-month average at its highest since March 2023.

The 10-year Treasury yield rose about 3 basis points to 5.311% after jumping as much as 7bp to 5.349% — its highest level since April 3, 2002; the 30-year touched 5.703%, a level not seen since late May 2002.
The Nasdaq closed at a record 27,477.31, up 1.05% (intraday high 27,544.07); the S&P 500 rose 0.66% to 7,773.95 and the Dow added 90.94 points (+0.18%) to 51,267.90.
'Tech is sort of like the inverse bond trade. It's buy tech, sell everything else,' Infrastructure Capital Advisors' Jay Hatfield said — calling the yield move 'a momentum selloff.'
Only 50.58% of Nasdaq Composite issues advanced on the record day; NYSE advancers still led decliners 1.04-to-1 and Nasdaq 1.09-to-1.

The euro fell to a 17-month low — its weakest since May 2025 — as France's deepening fiscal crisis and political uncertainty, plus speculation of an early election in Spain, pressured European assets; the dollar index rose ~0.2%.

chains.t: ② Oil's Supply Wave: G7 Barrels and Recovering Exports Push Brent to $100.32
steps: Brent settles -1.89% at $100.32; WTI settles at $89.43, down about 1.8% — a second straight supply-driven slide
The supply wave: the G7's 100M-barrel release (diesel first) adds barrels; Middle East exports topped pre-war levels on 4 of the last 7 days of September (Kpler/Vortexa)
Aramco cuts November prices for Asia to six-year lows; OPEC+ postpones its 2027 quota review
But the risk premium stays armed: Houthis claim missile and drone strikes on Aramco sites in Riyadh and Khurais; ING flags continued attacks on vessels
Products lead again: ICE gasoil +2% to $1,390.25 — Europe's diesel squeeze is still the complex's stress point
Ukraine will step up strikes on Russian refineries, Zelenskiy says — the supply war runs both ways
chains.d: For a second session the marginal oil headline was supply, not threat — G7 barrels, recovering exports, Aramco's price cut — and Brent's slide under $100.5 was the disinflation input equities used to wear a 5.31% 10-year.

news.fact: Brent crude futures fell 1.9% to close at $100.32 a barrel; US WTI settled at $89.43 a barrel, down about 1.8%.

Middle East crude exports have risen above pre-war levels on four of the last seven days of September (Kpler and Vortexa data), adding supply back into the market as the G7's 100-million-barrel release rolls out.

Yemen's Houthis said they fired missiles and drones at Saudi Aramco facilities in Riyadh and Khurais in response to Saudi-led strikes; separately, Aramco cut November prices for Asian buyers to six-year lows and OPEC+ delayed its 2027 quota review.
'We still see Brent remaining above $100 as long as tensions remain and attacks on vessels in the region continue,' ING analysts wrote; ICE gasoil futures rose 2% to $1,390.25.
Ukraine plans to step up attacks on Russian refineries, President Zelenskiy said — extending the war's supply risk to the other side of the barrel.

chains.t: ③ Deal Monday: Schneider's $22.6B Takeout of PTC — and Brazil's Election Rip
steps: Schneider Electric agrees to buy PTC in a $22.6B all-cash deal — PTC +33.5% to $192.26, the S&P 500's top performer and its largest one-day gain on record
C.H. Robinson to buy freight broker RXO for $5.8B in stock and cash — RXO +22.5%; C.H. Robinson -10.8%
Cerebras +9.1% after OpenAI's Sam Altman calls the chip designer a 'close partner'
Brazil's election shock: Bolsonaro leads the first round — the real +4%, Petrobras +11.5%, Ambev +8.7%
The ripple: Nu +13.0%, Bradesco +18.6%, Itaú +15.5% — Monday's widest winners were São Paulo's
chains.d: Monday's stock-picking came from the deal tape and a São Paulo ballot box — two multi-billion takeovers and Brazil's election repricing sorted the day's biggest winners.

news.fact: Schneider Electric agreed to acquire software maker PTC in an all-cash deal valuing its equity at about $22.6 billion; PTC closed up 33.5% — the top S&P 500 performer and its largest single-day gain on record.
RXO advanced 22.5% after C.H. Robinson Worldwide agreed to buy the freight broker for $5.8 billion in stock and cash; C.H. Robinson fell 10.8%.
Cerebras Systems gained 9.1% after OpenAI CEO Sam Altman called the chip designer a 'close partner' with 'deep engagement pushing on the frontiers of speed.'
Brazil's real jumped more than 4% as Bolsonaro led the first round of the presidential election; Petrobras gained 11.5% and Ambev 8.7% as Brazil-exposed names surged.

chains.t: ④ Under the Record: Thin Breadth, a Storage Bounce, and the Day's Laggards
steps: The record was thin: only ~50.6% of Nasdaq names advanced; the S&P logged 3 new 52-week highs against 18 new lows (Nasdaq: 23 vs 157)
The Dow's +0.18% and real estate's -0.3% show what didn't participate — Materials (+1.3%) and comm services (+1.2%) led instead
Laggards: Bristol Myers -3.8%, Nokia -3.8%, Corning -2.9%, Intel -2.6% — single-story and rate-pressed names got taxed
Storage bounced: Western Digital +6.3%, Seagate +4.5% — clawing back part of Friday's ~10% Toshiba shock
The split inside AI: the SOX was -0.3% early while software & services ran +1.4% — the stack trades name by name
chains.d: Under the record sat a narrow tape — half the Nasdaq up, more new lows than highs, the Dow barely green — and the day's money was made in deals, Brazil and a storage bounce, not in breadth.

news.fact: Only 50.58% of Nasdaq issues advanced on the record day, though advancing volume beat declining volume on both major exchanges.
The S&P 500 posted 3 new 52-week highs and 18 new lows; the Nasdaq Composite recorded 23 new highs and 157 new lows.
Bristol Myers Squibb, Nokia and Corning were among Monday's biggest large-cap decliners, each down roughly 3-4%.
Ten of 11 S&P sectors finished higher — Materials (+1.3%) and communication services (+1.2%) led, while real estate was the lone decliner.

chains.t: ⑤ The Relief Ledger: What Let Equities Wear a 5.31% 10-Year
steps: Oil's second straight supply-driven slide (Brent -1.9% to $100.32) is the quarter's cleanest disinflation input
Earnings hope carries: Goldman sees 27% Q3 EPS growth; 'the market still has enough momentum to push through' (Andersen Capital)
The near-term Fed trade stays dovish: ~80% odds of an October hold; December still largely priced (~70-84%)
The dollar's bid stayed orderly (DXY +0.2%) and gold barely moved — no panic signature anywhere
Gates ahead: Fed September minutes Wednesday; CPI Oct 14 — earnings open with Constellation (Tue), PepsiCo (Thu), Delta (Fri)
chains.d: Four shock absorbers — oil's supply slide, earnings optimism, a priced-out October hike and an orderly dollar — let the record happen despite the bond market.

news.fact: Traders see an 80% chance the Fed holds rates steady this month, though a December hike remains largely priced in, per CME FedWatch.
Goldman Sachs expects S&P 500 earnings growth of 27% year-over-year in Q3, underpinning the buy-the-dip camp; Citi's Beata Manthey: 'we still find ourselves in the resilience camp for now.'

'Many investors expect higher yields to derail the equity rally, but I think the market still has enough momentum to push through further increases in interest rates,' said Peter Andersen of Andersen Capital Management.
The week's gates: the Fed's September meeting minutes on Wednesday, CPI on Oct 14 — and earnings from Constellation Brands, PepsiCo and Delta Air Lines.

mtd.h: October, Three Sessions In: The Record Run Meets the 2002 Ceiling
mtd.d: S&P 7,651.5 to 7,773.95 (+1.60% MTD): a record run built on dovish repricing and deal tape, tested by a long end at fresh 2002 highs — plus the month's first supply wave for fuel.
mtd.c1: Three sessions into October, the month has its shape: a record run that won't wait for the bond market. The S&P is +1.60% MTD at 7,773.95 (within ~0.3% of its August record), the Nasdaq +2.29% with a record close, the Dow +0.71% — powered by the post-payrolls dovish repricing (~20% October hike odds), earnings optimism and a deal wave (PTC, RXO, Cerebras). Resisting it: a long end that printed fresh 2002 highs on both Oct 1 and Oct 5 — the 10Y at 5.31% (+2bp MTD), the 30Y at 5.66% (+3bp). Beneath: Energy (+3.2%) leads sectors, Health (-0.6%) lags; oil is -1.1% MTD as supply news (G7 barrels, recovering exports) met a still-armed risk premium; the dollar is +0.65% with the euro at a 17-month low; and gold, -0.7% MTD, still can't reclaim $4,200.
mtd.c4:
• October's checklist: Fed minutes (Wednesday), CPI (Oct 14), the Oct 28 meeting — with the near-term hike ~priced out, risk sits in any hawkish re-repricing.
  • The month's internal signature: growth (Tech, deals) leading while Health and rate-sensitives lag — dispersion, not direction.
  • $100 Brent is the month's line: supply policy is winning so far, but the risk premium re-arms on every escalation headline.

The month's next referees: Fed minutes (Wednesday), then CPI on Oct 14

news.fact: October hike odds sit near 20%, with traders seeing an 80% chance of a Fed hold this month; a December increase remains largely priced.
The Nasdaq reached an all-time high as megacap and growth stocks advanced, with Nvidia up ~1-2% and Meta, Microsoft and Tesla each up more than 1%.
Deal Monday: Schneider agreed to buy PTC for $22.6 billion and C.H. Robinson agreed to buy RXO for $5.8 billion — the month's first big takeovers.

chains.t: ② The Long End's Message: +2bp to 5.31%, and It Won't Blink
steps: The 10Y ends the window at 5.31%, +2bp MTD; the 30Y at 5.66%, +3bp
Both ends printed fresh multi-decade highs this month — including Monday's 5.349%/5.703% spikes
The steepening: 20Y +4bp and 30Y +4bp on Monday against a flat 2Y (4.82%) — term premium, not policy
France's debt burden and pre-election politics joined the global bond story
The dollar takes the yield bid: DXY +0.65% MTD to 102.11
chains.d: The month's most important number isn't a price — it's the 10Y's 5.31%: every equity gain this month is a bet against it.

news.fact: The 10-year yield touched 5.349% — its highest since April 2002 — and closed at 5.311%; the 30-year reached 5.703%, a level last seen in May 2002.
'Global bond markets were in focus on worries over France's debt burden and political uncertainty ahead of next year's presidential election.'
The euro fell to a 17-month low, its weakest since May 2025, as France's fiscal crisis and political uncertainty — and speculation of an early election in Spain — pressured European assets.

chains.t: ③ October's Two-Sided Trade: Dollars Firm, Oil Soft, Gold Stuck
steps: DXY +0.65% MTD at 102.11 — the yield gap still bids the dollar
WTI -1.1% MTD ($89.43) as the G7 release and recovering exports met the risk premium
Brent +2.4% MTD on the December basis ($100.32) — still above $100, off its Oct 1 peak
Gold -0.7% MTD ($4,156.8) — it can't reclaim $4,200 while real yields sit near multi-decade highs
Bitcoin +2.7% MTD ($85.8k) — the month's risk appetite shows up here, not in gold
chains.d: October's cross-asset tell: a firm dollar and soft crude — and gold, the cleanest dovish beneficiary, still can't hold a bid.

news.fact: Gold prices advanced on rising US debt worries and fading near-term hike expectations, but a firmer dollar capped gains; UBS's Giovanni Staunovo sees 'rising government debt levels as a structural tailwind' for bullion.
US gold futures settled 0.1% lower at $4,156.80 an ounce; spot gold edged 0.1% lower to $4,139.89.
Oil's slide extended as supply worries eased: Brent closed at $100.32 and WTI settled at $89.43.

qtd.h: Q4's First Three Sessions: +1.60% and a Record — the Data Wall Is Next
qtd.d: 9/30 7,651.5 to 10/5 7,773.95 (+1.60% QTD): Q4 opens with a Nasdaq record and a 5.31% 10Y — deals and AI carry while the rate-sensitive lag, and the data wall waits.
qtd.c1: Q4 is three sessions old and has both of its organizing themes: a record run (the Nasdaq's record close; the S&P +1.60% QTD at 7,773.95 — within ~0.3% of its August record) and a long end that won't join (the 10Y at 5.31%, fresh 2002 highs on both Oct 1 and Oct 5; the 30Y at 5.66%). The quarter opened on the post-payrolls dovish tilt (~20% October hike odds) and added a deal wave — Schneider/PTC ($22.6B), C.H. Robinson/RXO ($5.8B) — plus Brazil's election rip. Dispersion is the character so far: storage crashed ~10% Friday on Toshiba's capacity news, then bounced (WDC +6.3%, STX +4.5% Monday); real estate was Monday's only red sector; Energy (+3.2%) leads QTD, Health (-0.6%) lags. The quarter's first gates: Fed minutes (Wednesday), CPI (Oct 14), then the earnings wave (Constellation, PepsiCo, Delta).
qtd.c4:
• Q4's opening trade: 'no October hike' is nearly free to hold — the money is in December's repricing and earnings proof.
  • The dispersion signature: deals and AI get paid, rate-sensitives and guidance surprises get taxed — prove it or pay.
  • Duration: a 5.2%-5.35% 10Y band caps multiples while it lasts; the quarter's bull case starts with a bond market that stops making news.

news.fact: Q3 closed with the S&P up 2.03% and the Nasdaq up 2.47% — a second straight quarterly gain — while the Dow fell 2.70%.
The Nasdaq hit a new all-time high as AI-tied stocks rose — the quarter's first record close.

chains.d: Oil entered Q4 as the inflation stress point and got policy's answer within three sessions — but the risk premium stays armed above $100 Brent.

news.fact: The Trump administration told Germany and France to draw down emergency diesel inventories or face a potential US export ban.
The G7's 100M-barrel release and recovering exports pushed Brent to $100.32, down 1.9% on the day; Aramco cut November Asia prices to six-year lows.

ytd.h: The Bull Holds Into Q4: S&P +13.56% as the 10Y's +115bp Sets the Terms
ytd.d: S&P +13.56%, Nasdaq +18.22% (record), Dow +6.67% with three sessions of Q4 logged — AI and earnings carry; the 10Y's +115bp and an eighth month of war still tax the rest.
ytd.c1: Three sessions into Q4 and the year's base case is intact: the bull runs on AI capex and earnings proof, fighting the same two taxes — a 10Y up 115bp to 5.31% (fresh 2002 highs Monday) and oil up ~56% as the war grinds through its eighth month. The scoreboard: S&P +13.56%, Nasdaq +18.22% (record close), Dow +6.67%; underneath, energy (+41.9%) leads and consumer discretionary (-7.5%) lags. Monday added the quarter's first deal wave (Schneider/PTC, C.H. Robinson/RXO) and Brazil's election repricing — and kept the rate math honest: December still prices ~70-84% for a hike, with the Fed's minutes due Wednesday.
ytd.c4:
• The year's lesson holds into Q4: buy where earnings compound (AI infrastructure), rent where rates rule (long duration, the consumer).
  • Rates: the 10Y's +115bp is 2026's biggest tax — a confirmed Fed pause is the largest single bullish catalyst left this year.
  • Wildcards into year-end: the war's fuel premium (month eight) and December's Fed — both live.
